title: Farm Stand Route
story: A produce truck can bring fresh fruit and vegetables to a neighborhood once a week. UAB's mobile market has served more than 17,000 people since 2021. But a truck can only make a few stops, so where it parks matters a lot. In Woodlawn, many households have no car. Your job is to choose the four weekly stops, at churches, schools and libraries, so that more households with no car are within a 10-minute walk of fresh food. Walk times on the map are straight-line estimates.
residentQuote: The produce truck never comes to our side of the neighborhood.

levels.title: Place your first weekly farm-stand stop
levels.instructions: A function is a button you can press with code. `city.place_hub(...)` puts one weekly farm-stand stop on the map. Put the name of a place inside the parentheses, in quotes. Place one weekly farm-stand stop at Woodlawn Branch Library. Then press Run and watch the map.
levels.starterCode:
# Level 1: place one weekly farm-stand stop
# These two lines look at the first place on the list.
places = city.sites()
print(places[0])

# Your turn: call city.place_hub with the name of the place, in quotes.
hints: A function call has a name, then parentheses. What goes inside the parentheses is the thing the function should use. Names of places go in quotes.
Look at the line that starts with `print`. It already calls a function and puts something inside the parentheses. Your line looks the same, but it uses `city.place_hub` instead of `print`.

Here is a different problem. A lunch app has a function called `lunch.add_item`. To add an apple to the tray you would write: lunch.add_item("apple")  The function name comes first and the thing to add goes inside the parentheses, in quotes.

levels.title: Place four weekly farm-stand stops with a loop
levels.instructions: Writing `city.place_hub` 4 times is slow. A loop does the same job again and again for you. `city.sites()` gives you a list of places. Use a `for` loop to place a weekly farm-stand stop at the first 4 places on the list. Then press Run.
levels.starterCode:
# Level 2: place 4 weekly farm-stand stops with a loop
places = city.sites()
print("There are", len(places), "places to choose from.")

# Your turn: use a for loop to place a weekly farm-stand stop at the first 4 places.
hints: A `for` loop says: do this once for each thing in a list. Which list do you have? What should happen for each place?

A loop starts with `for something in a_list:` and the lines that repeat are indented under it. To use only the first few items of a list, you can cut it with square brackets, like `my_list[:3]`. You want 4.

Here is a different problem. You have a list of pets and want to say hello to the first 3:

pets = ["Milo", "Bean", "Pip", "Rex"]
for pet in pets[:3]:
    print("Hi", pet)

The word after `for` is a name you pick. It stands for one pet each time round the loop.

levels.title: Pick the 4 best places
levels.instructions: The first 4 places on the list are not always the best ones. Each place has `families_nearby`. Here that means households with no car within a 10-minute walk. Sort the places so the biggest number comes first. Then pick 4 weekly farm-stand stops from the top. One catch: the top places are often right next to each other, and two weekly farm-stand stops side by side help the same households. Skip a place if both its `lat` and its `lon` are less than 0.01 away from a place you already picked. Then press Run.
levels.starterCode:
# Level 4: sort, then choose
places = city.sites()
chosen = []   # the places you pick will go in here

# Step 1: sort places so the most families_nearby come first.
# Step 2: go down the sorted list. Pick a place unless it is
#         too close to one in chosen. Stop at 4.
# Remember to call city.place_hub for each place you pick.
hints: Do it in two parts. First, put the places in the right order. Then, choose from the top of the list. Try printing the first few sorted places. Where are they on the map?

To sort, use `sorted(list, key=..., reverse=True)`. The `key` tells Python which number to sort by. For each place you look at, ask: is it too close to anyone already in `chosen`? If not, add it to `chosen`.
